sm: Albert Mohler opens The Briefing for Monday, November 16, 2026, noting two huge headlines: the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, and a Friday shutdown of American airspace. The FAA grounded all aircraft after what was called a technological glitch, and about seven thousand flights were canceled or badly delayed, with recovery possibly lasting until Wednesday or Thursday. Mohler says no one was hurt and the shutdown was done safely, but it shows how dependent we are on technology. Officials blame a contractor replacing copper wire with fiber optic cable, and he says the aging air traffic system is a decades-long failure for which both parties share responsibility. Hacking was feared but probably was not the cause.

Mohler cites a New York Times Magazine article by James Fallows asking whether air travel is getting less safe. It notes almost sixteen years without a fatal commercial crash in the United States, ending with the January 2025 collision over the Potomac. He explains psychologist James Reason's Swiss cheese model, in which layered safeguards fail only when holes line up, so risk can be managed but never eliminated. He then turns to Jensen Huang. Huang admitted an affair with a woman, Alice Huang, who is unrelated to him and was suspected of acting for the Chinese government. She was reportedly watched by US authorities over suspicion that her company was a front for getting Nvidia chips to China. A second affair, with a direct report, then emerged.

Mohler says that once the second affair surfaced, Huang had to go. He observes that Silicon Valley's founders are so central that boards struggle to hold them accountable, and that Huang wrote the very company policy he violated. He says it is nearly impossible that Huang missed the concerns about Alice Huang. He quotes Stephen Witt in the New York Times on the reckless arrogance of Nvidia's leader and a narcissist's high, and notes a writer asking why smart men are so stupid. Mohler argues that Huang risked his marriage, his family, his company, national security and the economy, which leans heavily on the technology sector. From a Christian view, he says, sin blinds and makes us stupid, and the secular world underestimates it.

Mohler calls the story a sobering reminder of the exceeding sinfulness of sin and of the integrity of marriage vows, noting that few people respond by saying adultery is no big deal. The Economist wrote there has never been a scandal like this one and estimated Nvidia was worth perhaps five hundred billion dollars less than a week earlier. He says questions remain about what officials knew, possibly reaching the Commerce Department and the White House. He ties the story to other fragile systems, including a Microsoft Outlook outage that week. He closes with a counterpoint, SpaceX catching its returning Starship rocket with the tower's arms, showing both human achievement and human failure.
